title: Africa’s Energy Curse Is a Political Choice
gist: Africa sits on 125 billion barrels of oil and 620+ trillion cubic feet of gas while 600 million of its people lack electricity, and the authors argue this is a deliberate political choice by elites who prefer hard-currency export revenues over domestic electrification. Corruption (roughly 15% of windfalls captured offshore), below-cost energy subsidies, and Europe's post-Ukraine scramble for African gas all reinforce export orientation, but Africa is projected to flip from net energy exporter to net importer by the early 2030s.

insights.claim: Africa holds roughly 125 billion barrels of confirmed oil reserves and more than 620 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, with vast additional deposits still undiscovered.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: The resource base is large enough that African supply decisions are a swing variable for Atlantic-basin LNG and crude balances, not a rounding error.
insights.quote: The continent holds roughly 125 billion barrels of confirmed oil reserves and more than 620 trillion cubic feet of natural gas

insights.claim: Some 600 million Africans have no electricity at home, a figure that has not fallen since the COVID-19 pandemic and is projected to still exceed half a billion in 2030.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: A stalled electrification curve means the addressable market for distributed power, gensets and grid equipment is not shrinking — and signals policy failure rather than demand saturation.
insights.quote: some 600 million Africans have no electricity at home, and this figure has not fallen since the COVID-19 pandemic
insights.locator: At the same time, some 600 million

insights.claim: The gap between African energy abundance and African energy deprivation is a political problem rather than a geological one, because every exported barrel or contracted LNG cargo is energy deliberately withheld from domestic households, hospitals and factories.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Frames African supply risk as governance risk: reform, not new drilling, is the variable that changes the export trajectory.
insights.quote: The problem is not geological, but political.

insights.claim: Nigeria alone holds enough natural gas to achieve 100% electrification within its own borders, and gas-to-power projects across Africa have long demonstrated technical viability.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Technical feasibility is not the binding constraint on African gas-to-power; pricing and institutions are, which is where policy catalysts would show up.
insights.quote: Nigeria holds enough natural gas to achieve 100% electrification within its borders
insights.locator: But the case for domestic use

insights.claim: The International Energy Agency estimates universal electricity access in Africa requires $15 billion of annual investment for ten years, while only $2.5 billion is currently committed each year.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: A roughly $12.5 billion annual financing gap defines the size of any credible African power-investment theme — and how far current commitments fall short.
insights.quote: achieving universal electricity access in Africa would require annual investments of $15 billion for ten years, and though only $2.5 billion is currently being committed each year

themes.theme: Rent Capture and the Corruption Discount

insights.claim: Exporting a barrel and converting a barrel into domestic electricity are economically equivalent only if governance is sound and pricing is free — two conditions that have not been met in African producer states.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Gives a two-variable test — institutional quality and price liberalization — for judging whether any resource-rich country's export strategy actually compounds national wealth.
insights.quote: A barrel exported at world prices and a barrel converted into electricity should produce the same national wealth if governance is sound and pricing is free.

insights.claim: Nigeria has generated more than $600 billion in oil revenues since the 1960s while simultaneously recording one of the world's highest rates of extreme poverty.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Half a century of evidence that Nigerian oil revenue does not transmit to domestic demand — a caution for consumer-growth theses built on commodity upcycles.
insights.quote: Nigeria has generated more than $600 billion in oil revenues since the 1960s while also recording one of the world’s highest rates of extreme poverty.

insights.claim: Equatorial Guinea achieved Africa's highest per capita GDP during oil-boom years even as more than half its population lived below the poverty line.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Per capita GDP is a broken proxy for domestic purchasing power in petrostates; use electrification and household metrics instead.
insights.quote: During oil-boom years, Equatorial Guinea has achieved the continent’s highest per capita GDP even as over half of its population lives below the poverty line.

insights.claim: Research tracking offshore bank accounts finds that around 15% of windfall gains flowing to petroleum-producing countries with weak institutional safeguards ends up in the hands of those in power.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: A quantified leakage rate lets investors haircut the domestic multiplier of any commodity windfall in weak-institution jurisdictions by roughly a sixth before it even reaches the budget.
insights.quote: around 15% of windfall gains flowing to petroleum-producing countries with weak institutional safeguards ends up in the pockets of those in power
insights.locator: All told, research tracking offshore bank accounts

insights.claim: Below-cost domestic fuel and power prices in African producer states are not accidents but core instruments of petrostate political economy — a diffuse benefit offered to populations who otherwise see none of the extracted wealth.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Explains why subsidy reform repeatedly stalls despite IMF pressure: removing it strips the regime's only broad-based legitimacy transfer.
insights.quote: They are core instruments of the petrostate political economy: a diffuse benefit handed to populations who otherwise see little of the wealth nominally being extracted on their behalf.

insights.claim: Nigeria's domestic gas prices have historically been held so low that building a gas-fired power plant is commercially pointless.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Price caps, not capital scarcity, block Nigerian IPP investment — watch domestic gas price liberalization as the trigger for a power-build cycle.
insights.quote: Nigeria’s domestic gas prices have historically been held so low that building a gas-fired power plant is commercially pointless.
insights.locator: Domestic energy subsidies are a second distortion

insights.claim: Angola has the world's fourth-cheapest retail gasoline, an example of African producer states charging consumers far less for fuel and electricity than actual cost.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Deep fuel subsidies are a hidden fiscal liability that expands when crude prices rise, inverting the usual petrostate windfall logic.
insights.quote: Angola has the world’s fourth-cheapest retail gasoline.
insights.locator: In many African producer states, consumers pay

insights.claim: Subsidies send a false price signal that makes energy exports appear economically superior to domestic use even when the welfare arithmetic points the other way.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Investment decisions in these markets are being made off distorted prices, so apparent export-project returns overstate true national returns.
insights.quote: But subsidies also send a false signal to investors and governments, making energy exports appear economically superior to domestic use, even when the welfare arithmetic says otherwise.
insights.locator: But subsidies also send a false signal

themes.theme: Europe's Post-Ukraine Scramble for African Gas

insights.claim: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine severed roughly 80 billion cubic meters of annual gas supply to Europe, and a Middle East war in 2026 tightened LNG markets further, sending European governments to Algiers, Dakar and Maputo in search of supply.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Two consecutive supply shocks have structurally reoriented European gas procurement toward African suppliers, supporting long-dated African export contracts.
insights.quote: Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine severed some 80 billion cubic meters of annual gas supplies to Europe, and this year’s Middle East war tightened LNG markets further.
insights.locator: Recent geopolitical shocks are a third factor

insights.claim: Algeria became the European Union's second-largest pipeline gas supplier in 2023 with 20% of pipeline imports, behind Norway at 54% and ahead of Russia at 17%.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Algeria's pipeline share now exceeds Russia's, making Algerian political stability a first-order European energy-security exposure.
insights.quote: Algeria became the European Union’s second-largest pipeline gas supplier in 2023, providing 20% of pipeline imports, behind Norway at 54% and ahead of Russia at 17%.

insights.claim: A new gas project off Mauritania and Senegal shipped its first cargo to Atlantic markets in 2025, and Angola has redirected LNG cargoes westward.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: New West African supply is landing in Atlantic-basin markets, adding competition to US Gulf Coast LNG into Europe.
insights.quote: a new project off Mauritania and Senegal shipped its first cargo to Atlantic markets in 2025
insights.locator: Angola has directed LNG cargoes westward

insights.claim: European demand has handed African producer governments political cover, letting a 20-year gas export commitment be framed as diplomatic solidarity rather than as a decision taken at the expense of domestic electrification.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Long-term European offtake deals lock in export orientation for two decades, raising the odds of later domestic-political backlash and contract renegotiation risk.
insights.quote: Committing gas to Europe for 20 years can be framed as an act of solidarity and diplomacy, rather than as a choice made at the expense of domestic electrification.
insights.locator: For African producers, the windfall has come

insights.claim: European governments spent more than $640 billion shielding their citizens from Ukraine-crisis energy prices, and part of that spending flowed through to African producer-government revenues that accrue to elites rather than to households without power.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: European consumer-protection fiscal spending indirectly financed rent capture abroad — a second-order cost rarely counted in energy-security budgets.
insights.quote: European governments spend more than $640 billion shielding their citizens from the price consequences of the Ukraine crisis
insights.locator: There is a bitter irony here

insights.claim: Africa's population will reach 2.5 billion by 2050 and domestic energy demand is rising fast enough that the continent is projected to shift from net energy exporter to net importer by the early 2030s.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: If Africa flips to net importer within roughly five years, long-dated African export contracts and the seaborne supply models built on them face structural erosion.
insights.quote: Africa is projected to shift from a net energy exporter to a net importer by the early 2030s

insights.claim: The global energy transition is narrowing the window in which African oil and gas can still be exported at high prices to willing international buyers.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Time-limited monetization raises the option value of front-loading African export volumes but also the stranded-asset risk on late-cycle projects.
insights.quote: the global energy transition is narrowing the window through which oil and gas can be exported at high prices to willing international buyers

insights.claim: A young, urban, electricity-dependent African population facing persistent blackouts in visibly resource-rich countries is not a politically sustainable configuration, so change will come either through deliberate reform or through instability.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Political risk in African petrostates is structurally rising; the binary between reform and instability should widen country-risk spreads over the next decade.
insights.quote: It is not politically sustainable to have a young, urban, electricity-dependent population confronting persistent blackouts in countries that are visibly resource-rich.

insights.claim: The export-versus-electrification tradeoff is almost never debated openly in African producer states, and citizens are not told what choices are being made in their name, by whom, or for whose benefit.
insights.speaker: RABAH AREZKI
insights.so_what: Transparency of allocation decisions is the leading indicator to watch — public debate would precede any real reallocation of hydrocarbons toward domestic power.
insights.quote: This silence is a political choice, and ending it is where any serious reform must begin.
